lessons.title: Here-documents, here-strings and process substitution
lessons.goal:
Feed text to commands without temporary files, and compare or merge the output of commands as if they were files.

Why it matters: these three features remove most temporary files from scripts, avoid the lost-variable trap of `cmd | while read`, and make one-liners such as `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)` possible.

setup.note: Scripts are saved in a scratch directory. No special tools are needed.

steps.title: Here-document
steps.text: `<<EOF ... EOF` gives the lines in between as **standard input**. With an unquoted delimiter, variables and `$(...)` are expanded; with a **quoted** delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) nothing is. `<<-` strips leading tabs so you can indent.

run.cmd:
name=Linux; cat <<EOF
Hello, $name!
Today is a $(date +%A | sed 's/.*/day/').
EOF
run.output:
Hello, Linux!
Today is a day.

run.cmd:
cat > config.ini <<EOF
[server]
port=8080
EOF
grep -c = config.ini

steps.after: Here-documents are the standard way to write a config file or send a multi-line message from a script.

steps.title: Here-string
steps.text: `<<< "text"` feeds one string (plus a newline) as stdin. It is handy with `read` and `grep`.

run.cmd: read -r first rest <<< 'alpha beta gamma'; echo "first=$first rest=$rest"

steps.title: The pipe-to-while trap
steps.text: Each part of a pipeline runs in a **subshell**. A variable set in a `while read` at the end of a pipe is lost when the loop ends.

run.cmd:
count=0; printf 'a
b
c
' | while read -r l; do count=$((count + 1)); done; echo "count after the pipe: $count"

steps.title: Process substitution
steps.text: `<(cmd)` runs `cmd` and gives its output a **file name** (`/dev/fd/N`) that other programs can open. With `done < <(cmd)` the loop runs in the **current** shell, so variables survive. `>(cmd)` is the same for output.

run.cmd:
count=0; while read -r l; do count=$((count + 1)); done < <(printf 'a
b
c
'); echo "count with process substitution: $count"

steps.under: Bash creates a pipe (or a named FIFO), starts `cmd` with its output connected to it, and substitutes `/dev/fd/N`, the path of the read end in the shell's own descriptor table. That is why the receiving program sees a normal file name. Programs that need a seekable file (not a stream) cannot read it.

steps.title: Compare outputs without temporary files
steps.text: `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)` compares two sorted listings; `comm -12 <(sort a) <(sort b)` shows the lines common to both; `paste <(cmd1) <(cmd2)` puts outputs side by side.

run.cmd: diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt); echo "diff exit status: $?"
printf 'x\ny\n' | tee >(wc -l | sed 's/^/lines: /') >(tr a-z A-Z | sed 's/^/upper: /') > /dev/null; sleep 0.3

options: No expansion of variables or commands in the body

quiz.q: Why does `echo hi | read v; echo $v` print nothing?
options: `read` runs in a subshell and the variable is lost
A file name (/dev/fd/N) from which the output can be read

quiz.q: Which form keeps variables set in the loop?
quiz.explain: The loop runs in the current shell.

check.scenario: Compare the installed packages of two servers with one command, given `ssh` access.
check.answer: `diff <(ssh server1 'rpm -qa | sort') <(ssh server2 'rpm -qa | sort')`. Each `ssh` runs concurrently and its sorted output appears as a file to `diff`; no temporary files are needed.

lessons.title: Option parsing with getopts, and debugging scripts
lessons.goal:
Parse command-line options the standard way, and find bugs with `bash -x`, `bash -n`, `PS4` and traps.

Why it matters: scripts that accept options correctly feel like real tools, and tracing shows what bash actually runs, which ends most guessing.

setup.note: Scripts are saved in a scratch directory. No special tools are needed.

steps.title: A script with options
steps.text: `getopts ":vn:c:h" opt` loops over options: `v` and `h` are flags, `n:` and `c:` take an argument (stored in `$OPTARG`). The leading `:` selects quiet error handling, so you print your own messages. `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` leaves the remaining arguments.

run.output:
verbose mode on
hello Linux (1)
hello Linux (2)
files: a.txt b.txt

steps.title: Errors in the options
steps.text: A missing argument and an unknown option reach the `:` and `?` branches.

run.output:
option -n needs an argument
exit status: 2

verbose mode on
hello world (1)
hello world (2)
hello world (3)
files: f
options may be combined: -vc3

steps.title: Trace with bash -x
steps.text: `bash -x script` prints every command **after expansion**, prefixed with `+`. It shows the real arguments, the branch taken and the values of variables. Set `PS4` to add the line number and file.

run.output:
+ 4: verbose=0
+ 4: name=world
+ 4: count=1
+ 5: getopts :vn:c:h opt
+ 6: case $opt in
+ 8: name=x
+ 5: getopts :vn:c:h opt
+ 15: shift 2

steps.title: Check syntax without running
steps.text: `bash -n` parses the script and reports syntax errors without executing anything. Always run it on scripts that change systems.

run.cmd: printf 'if true; then\n  echo ok\n' > broken.sh; bash -n broken.sh 2>&1 | sed 's/^broken.sh: //'; echo "exit status: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
run.output:
line 3: syntax error: unexpected end of file
exit status: 2

steps.title: Trace only a part, and trap errors
steps.text: `set -x` and `set +x` switch tracing on for a section. `trap ... ERR` runs when a command fails; `$LINENO` and `$BASH_COMMAND` tell where and what.

run.cmd: bash -c 'echo before; set -x; x=$((2 + 3)); echo "x=$x"; set +x; echo after' 2>&1
run.output:
before
+ x=5
+ echo x=5
x=5
+ set +x
after

run.cmd: bash -c 'trap "echo failed at line \$LINENO: \$BASH_COMMAND" ERR; true; false; echo continues'

steps.under: `getopts` handles only **short** options. For long options (`--name=x`) scripts use a manual `case` loop over `"$@"`, or the external `getopt` command (GNU). Also useful for debugging: `set -o functrace` (traps in functions), `declare -p VAR` (show a variable's attributes and value), `type FUNC` (show a function's code), and `bash --debugger`/`bashdb` for a real debugger.

quiz.q: What does the leading colon in `getopts ":vn:"` do?
options: Quiet error handling: you print the messages
Each command after expansion, with a + prefix
quiz.explain: A trace of what really runs.

quiz.q: How do you check a script's syntax without running it?

options: The index of the next argument; shift by OPTIND-1 to get the positional arguments

check.scenario: A script behaves differently under cron than in your terminal. How do you debug it?
check.answer: Make cron's environment visible: `bash -x script.sh > /tmp/script.trace 2>&1` from the crontab (or add `set -x` and a log file via `exec > >(tee -a /tmp/log) 2>&1`), print `env | sort` and `PATH`, use absolute paths, and compare the trace with a run from `env -i /bin/bash --noprofile --norc script.sh` which imitates cron's empty environment.

interview.a: `<(cmd)` presents the output of cmd as a file (/dev/fd/N); `>(cmd)` does the same for input. Lets tools that need files read command output, and keeps loops in the current shell. See [the lesson](#/lesson/46/heredocs-process-substitution).

interview.q: Why does a variable set in `cmd | while read` disappear?
interview.a: The loop runs in a subshell. Use `while read ...; done < <(cmd)` or `shopt -s lastpipe` in non-interactive scripts.

interview.q: What does a here-document with a quoted delimiter do?
interview.a: It passes the text literally: no variable, command or arithmetic expansion.

interview.q: How do you parse options in bash?
interview.a: `getopts` for short options in a while loop, then `shift $((OPTIND-1))`; a manual case loop or GNU getopt for long options. See [the lesson](#/lesson/46/getopts-and-debugging).

interview.q: How do you debug a shell script?
interview.a: `bash -x` (trace), `PS4` with LINENO, `bash -n` (syntax check), `set -x/+x` around a section, `trap ... ERR`, shellcheck.
Runs both sorts, exposes their outputs as files and diffs them without temporary files.

glossary.def: Multi-line text given to a command as standard input with <<DELIM.
A single string fed as standard input with <<<.
<(cmd) or >(cmd): a command's output or input presented as a file name.
A bash builtin that parses short command-line options.
Index of the next argument to be processed by getopts.
The prompt printed before each command in a set -x trace.

commands.desc: Loop over command output in the current shell.
